title: The Three Cases (Aḥwāl al-Iʿrāb)
source: Original instructional lesson authored for this application (syllabus ref: Haywood & Nahmad Ch. 4; Ryding Ch. 3 §3.9, Ch. 8 §§8.1–8.4)
objectives: Identify the three nominal cases: Nominative (rafʿ), Accusative (naṣb), and Genitive (jarr).
Vocalize definite and indefinite singular nouns across all three cases.
Apply the accusative alif spelling rule and recognize prepositions governing jarr.
recallPrompt: From Chapter 3: Why does وَاسِعَةٌ take ة in الأَرْضُ وَاسِعَةٌ?

sections.heading: Why Case Endings Matter in Classical Arabic
sections.body: In Classical Arabic, a noun's final short vowel signals its syntactic role in the sentence. There are three nominal cases: Nominative (rafʿ / marfūʿ) for subjects and predicates; Accusative (naṣb / manṣūb) for direct objects and adverbials; and Genitive (jarr / majrūr) after prepositions and in annexation (iḍāfah).

sections.label: Threefold Singular Declension
sections.summary: Definite singular nouns end in -u (nom.), -a (acc.), and -i (gen.). Indefinite singular nouns end in -un, -an, and -in, with an added silent alif (ـًا) in the indefinite accusative (except after ة or ء preceded by ا).

sections.heading: Case Markers on Singular Triptote Nouns

sections.translation: The student is in the mosque.
sections.irab: الطَّالِبُ: مُبْتَدَأٌ مَرْفُوعٌ بِالضَّمَّةِ | فِي: حَرْفُ جَرٍّ | المَسْجِدِ: اسْمٌ مَجْرُورٌ بِفِي وَعَلَامَةُ جَرِّهِ الكَسْرَةُ
sections.notes: The preposition فِي governs المَسْجِدِ in the genitive case, marked by kasrah (-i).

sections.heading: Accusative Alif Exception
sections.body: Indefinite accusative nouns ending in tāʾ marbūṭah (e.g., مَدِينَةً) or hamzah after alif (e.g., سَمَاءً) take fatḥatān directly without adding a trailing alif.
